strengths: The paper gives a clean formalization of correctness-based RL as latent-generation maximum likelihood. The Maclaurin expansion log p = -sum_{k>=1}(1-p)^k/k and the resulting population-level weight-function view (Section 3, Section 5, Table 2) provide a useful unifying perspective: RL optimizes only the first-order pass@k term, while MaxRL interpolates toward maximum likelihood as sampling compute increases.

The estimator-objective equivalence is elegant and correctly proven for the estimator in Eq. (9): normalizing score functions by the number of successful rollouts K yields an unbiased gradient for the truncated MaxRL objective with T=N (Theorem 2). The conditional-gradient interpretation in Theorem 1 is simple and intuitive.

The empirical evaluation is extensive and spans controlled, small-scale, and large-scale settings: ImageNet with exact maximum likelihood (Figure 2), infinite-data maze navigation (Figure 3, Table 3), data-scarce GSM8K training (Figure 4, Table 4), and Qwen3-1.7B/4B reasoning training (Figure 5). The results convincingly show improved pass@k, reduced pass@k collapse, and large test-time efficiency gains over GRPO in several settings.

The paper is well written and positions itself clearly relative to RLVR, pass@k optimization, and closely related work such as Xiong et al. (2025b) and Davis and Recht (2025). Limitations are acknowledged (binary reward, on-policy setting, no continuous/multi-turn rewards).
weaknesses: The practical Algorithm 1 drops both terms of the control-variate estimator when K=0. This breaks exact unbiasedness for the truncated MaxRL objective, because the second term -(1/N)sum S_i is zero-mean only unconditionally; conditional on K>0 it is not generally zero-mean. Thus the paper's 'unbiased estimator' claim applies to Eq. (9), but not exactly to the implemented algorithm. The authors should either retain the zero-mean term when K=0 or explicitly characterize the resulting bias.

There is no finite-sample variance analysis or bound for the proposed estimator. The 1/K normalization can have high variance when successes are rare, and the control-variate variance reduction is asserted rather than quantified. This is important because the method's practical advantage depends on stable optimization under sparse successes.

Experimental results generally lack error bars or multiple seeds, including the maze, GSM8K, and Qwen3 training runs. Some large-scale comparisons only evaluate against GRPO, not other RL objectives such as RLOO. This limits the statistical strength of the empirical claims, even though the observed gaps are often large.

The population-level GRPO weighting derivation in Section 5/Appendix C treats the empirical group mean and standard deviation as if they were population quantities. Finite-sample correlations between the normalization and the score functions are not discussed, so the derived 1/sqrt(p(1-p)) weighting is an asymptotic or infinite-group approximation rather than an exact finite-sample objective.

There are several presentation issues and typos: e.g., 'making the resulting estimator no longer unbiased with respect to Eq. (9)' should likely refer to Eq. (8); 'PKPO (T-16) (Walter and Kuhlmann, 2025)' appears to mis-cite Walder and Karkhanis (2025); 'GRPO (with outage beam)' likely means entropy bonus. The term 'Pareto-dominates' is used somewhat loosely when some training curves initially lag baselines.

strengths: Clean and correct theoretical framing. I verified the Maclaurin expansion (Eq. 4-5): since fail@k(x) = (1-p)^k, log p = -Σ(1-p)^k/k and ∇log p = Σ (1/k)∇pass@k, so the claim that expected-reward RL retains only the first-order term is mathematically sound. This gives a nice, unifying reinterpretation of RL vs ML in binary-reward settings.

Theorems 1 and 2 are correct and the proofs (Appendix B) check out. Theorem 1 (ML gradient = success-conditioned expected score) and Theorem 2 (the 1/K-normalized estimator is unbiased for the truncated objective at order T=N) constitute a genuinely clean finite-sample estimator–objective equivalence: E[ĝ_N] = pass@N · ∇log p = ∇J_MaxRL^(N). The alignment between 'more rollouts' and 'higher-order objective' is an elegant point.

The unifying weight-function view (Eq. 11, Table 2, Figure 1) is a real conceptual contribution. Expressing RL (w=1), GRPO (w=1/√(p(1-p))), MaxRL (w=(1-(1-p)^T)/p) and ML (w=1/p) on a common axis clarifies why GRPO upweights mid-difficulty prompts and inverts at high pass rate, and situates MaxRL as an interpolation toward ML.

The method is simple and practical: a one-line change in advantage normalization ((r-μ̂)/μ̂ instead of /σ̂ or leave-one-out). This makes the contribution easy to adopt in existing on-policy pipelines.

Broad empirical evaluation across four regimes of increasing realism: didactic ImageNet (where exact ML is available), a 3M-parameter transformer on 1M procedurally generated mazes (infinite-data), SmolLM2-360M on GSM8K (data-scarce), and Qwen3-1.7B/4B on math reasoning. Improvements over GRPO/RLOO are consistent and often large (e.g., maze pass@1 84.4 vs 43.6; GSM8K pass@1024 83.4 vs 48.6).

The pass@k preservation and test-time scaling results (up to ~20× efficiency with a perfect verifier) address a practically important problem (RLVR diversity collapse) and are supported by an appropriate coverage-based analysis.
Limitations are stated honestly (binary reward only, no continuous/multi-turn/off-policy extension).
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty relative to what is claimed. The core identity ∇J_ML = success-conditioned expected score is acknowledged as a recent observation by Davis and Recht (2025), and the Maclaurin expansion is a reformulation rather than a new derivation. The central new result (Theorem 2) is a short consequence of Theorem 1 plus the pass@N factor, so the 'principled framework' framing oversells the technical depth.

No error bars or multiple seeds for any experiment, including the billion-parameter Qwen3 runs. RL fine-tuning is notoriously high-variance, and the paper makes strong 'Pareto-dominates in all models and tasks' claims with single runs. This is a material evidential gap for the headline conclusion.

The practical estimator (Algorithm 1) deviates from the theoretical one: dropping the control variate when K=0 makes the implemented gradient unbiased for order T=N-1 rather than T=N (I derived E[ĝ_alg] = ∇J_MaxRL^(N-1)). The paper calls this 'simpler and performs better empirically' but does not analyze the objective mismatch it introduces.

The ImageNet 'exact ML' experiment trains ResNet-50 from scratch, where the initial pass rate is ~0.1% and REINFORCE's failure is an expected artifact of sparse-reward learning from random initialization rather than a meaningful indictment of the RL objective. The comparison is closer to a strawman than a decisive test (though the authors partially caveat this).

Overclaiming in the abstract/introduction ('Pareto-dominates existing methods in all models and tasks we tested', 'up to 20× gains') without qualification about seeds, task scope, or the asymptotic nature of the ML approximation.

The truncated objective underweights very hard inputs relative to true ML: the weight saturates at T for p ≲ 1/T rather than scaling as 1/p. Thus 'approaches ML' is purely asymptotic and may mislead at realistic finite rollout budgets — the regime where hard problems matter most.

The large maze/GSM8K gaps versus GRPO partly reflect GRPO's well-documented pass@k collapse, so the gains may be as much about avoiding a known pathology as about a uniquely superior objective. Diversity-preserving baselines (PKPO, differential smoothing, entropy bonus) are relegated to tables/appendix and not integrated into the main scaling curves.

Reproducibility is only partial: hyperparameters are provided, but no code release is indicated and training requires large-scale hardware (e.g., 32×H200), limiting independent verification. There are also citation/notation errors (e.g., 'Walder and Karkhanis' vs 'Walter and Kuhlmann'; 'PKPO (T-16)'; inconsistent MaxRL/MAXRL and pass@k/pass@K).

strengths: Provides a clean theoretical bridge: formalizes binary-reward RL as latent-generation maximum likelihood and shows via a Maclaurin expansion that the standard RL gradient is only the first-order term of the log pass-rate gradient. This gives a principled explanation for why RLVR can underweight hard prompts.

Introduces a compute-indexed family J_MaxRL^(T) that exactly interpolates between expected reward (T=1) and maximum likelihood (T->infinity), and derives a simple success-normalized REINFORCE estimator whose expectation matches the gradient of the truncated ML objective for T=N. The estimator-objective equivalence is elegant and makes additional rollouts improve the objective itself, not merely reduce variance.

The unifying weight-function view (Table 2, Figure 1) is illuminating: RL has w(p)=1, GRPO has w(p)=1/sqrt(p(1-p)), MaxRL has w(p)=(1-(1-p)^T)/p, and ML has w(p)=1/p. This clarifies GRPO's pass@k degradation and MaxRL's emphasis on low-pass-rate prompts.

The algorithm is extremely simple: a one-line change in advantage normalization (divide by per-prompt mean reward) that can be dropped into existing on-policy RL pipelines, with no value network, KL penalty, or entropy bonus required in the reported experiments.

Empirical breadth is strong: controlled ImageNet experiments where exact ML is available, a 3M-parameter maze transformer with 1M unique mazes, SmolLM2-360M on GSM8K for 50 epochs, and Qwen3-1.7B/4B on four math benchmarks. MaxRL improves both pass@1 and pass@k, resists overfitting, and yields up to roughly 20x test-time scaling efficiency.

Optimization-dynamics analysis is insightful: gradient-norm-vs-pass-rate plots show MaxRL concentrates learning signal on hard prompts like cross-entropy, whereas GRPO peaks at medium difficulty and RLOO/REINFORCE are nearly flat. MaxRL also produces more prompts with at least one correct rollout during training.

Limitations are honestly acknowledged in the conclusion: binary rewards, on-policy training, and single-turn settings are the current scope, with continuous rewards, multi-turn RL, and off-policy methods left for future work. Hyperparameters, architectures, datasets, and hardware are reported in detail, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is partly incremental: the conditional form of the ML gradient and mean-reward normalization have been recently noted by Davis and Recht (2025), Xiong et al. (2025b), and Huang et al. (2025). The main new contribution is the finite-sample estimator-objective equivalence, but the manuscript should sharpen exactly how much this advances beyond concurrent work.

The claim that maximum likelihood is 'the principled objective' is somewhat overstated. All objectives considered are monotone transformations of per-input pass rate and share the same global optimum p=1 under unlimited capacity; the benefit is a finite-capacity and optimization-dynamics effect, not a different global objective. The 1/p weighting may also be undesirable under noisy verifiers or label noise, which is not tested.

The empirical claim that MaxRL 'Pareto-dominates existing methods in all models and tasks' is not literally true at every training point: in GSM8K Figure 4 MaxRL trails GRPO at early pass@1, and some Qwen3 curves are close. The paper should state final-checkpoint or asymptotic dominance rather than universal Pareto dominance.

Baseline fairness could be strengthened. All methods are trained in a simplified on-policy setup without KL regularization, entropy bonus, or clipping, whereas GRPO often depends on these components. Although some GRPO+entropy results appear in tables, broader hyperparameter tuning and sensitivity analyses (e.g., epsilon in the denominator, rollout count, learning rate) are missing, and PKPO/differential-smoothing baselines use fixed hyperparameters.

The test-time scaling efficiency gains (e.g., 20x) are not precisely defined in the main text. The metric likely compares sample counts needed to reach a given coverage, but the calculation is deferred and may be sensitive to the pass@k estimator and benchmark sampling variance, especially for very large k such as 1024 or 4096.

Reproducibility is good but incomplete: no code release or detailed pseudocode for the custom maze rollout engine is provided. The treatment of the control variate when K=0 also differs between Eq. (10) and Algorithm 1, which could confuse reimplementation even though both choices remain unbiased.

Presentation has issues: typos such as 'MaxRL show' and 'outage beam' (likely 'entropy bonus'), and the reference list appears corrupted with incorrect author-year labels (e.g., Boerner et al. (2023) for Bishop (2006), Auer et al. (2025) for Auer et al. (2002)), making citations difficult to verify.

strengths: Provides a clean and illuminating theoretical connection between binary-reward reinforcement learning and maximum likelihood: the Maclaurin expansion of log pass rate in terms of pass@k events shows that standard expected-reward RL optimizes only the first-order term, while MaxRL interpolates to ML as rollouts increase.

Theorem 1 gives a useful conditional-expectation form of the ML gradient over successful trajectories, and Theorem 2 establishes an elegant unbiased estimator-objective equivalence: normalizing score functions by the number of successful rollouts yields an unbiased estimator for the truncated ML gradient of order T=N.

The practical algorithm is a simple one-line change to standard RL implementations (advantage normalization by the per-prompt mean reward instead of standard deviation), making it easy to adopt and test.

Extensive empirical evaluation across ImageNet, procedural mazes, GSM8K, and Qwen3-1.7B/4B mathematical reasoning shows consistent improvements in pass@1, pass@k, and test-time scaling efficiency over GRPO and RLOO.

The paper includes many additional baseline comparisons in the appendix (PKPO, ZPD, Power Function, entropy bonus, differential smoothing, SELF), which strengthens the empirical case beyond just GRPO/RLOO.

The weight-function view (Table 2, Figure 1) provides a unified population-level interpretation of RL, GRPO, MaxRL, and ML, clarifying how objectives differ in their emphasis on easy vs. hard prompts.

Limitations are discussed honestly, including the restriction to binary rewards, the lack of off-policy/multi-turn extensions, and the issue that prompts with zero successful rollouts receive no gradient.
Code and detailed hyperparameters are released, and the experimental protocols for the main settings are described in enough detail for reproduction.
weaknesses: Algorithm 1 line 8 appears inconsistent with Eq. (10) and Theorem 5: it multiplies by $\widehat{r}(x)$ rather than dividing by it, which introduces an extra factor of $\widehat{r}(x)^2$ relative to the intended estimator. The correct implementation (advantage $(r-\text{mean})/\text{mean}$) is given in Appendix F, but the main algorithm as written is not the estimator analyzed theoretically, undermining the central 'one-line change' claim and risking reproducibility issues.

The claim that MaxRL 'Pareto-dominates existing methods in all tested models and tasks' is overstated. In the GSM8K experiment MaxRL has slower initial gains than GRPO/RLOO, and in some large-model benchmarks (e.g., MATH-500 with Qwen3-1.7B) pass@1 is similar or slightly lower, so strict Pareto dominance does not hold at all training stages or metrics. At LLM scale, the main text compares mainly to GRPO rather than a broad set of baselines.

The experiments do not fully isolate the source of improvement. MaxRL produces longer chain-of-thought responses and retains higher entropy during training, and the paper does not control for these factors at the Qwen3 scale. A GRPO+entropy-bonus baseline is only reported in smaller settings, so it remains possible that some gains come from implicit entropy/length regularization rather than the MaxRL objective itself.

The reported test-time scaling efficiency gains (up to 20x) are striking but lack confidence intervals or statistical significance tests. Some benchmarks (e.g., AIME 2025) contain only 30 problems, and pass@k estimates at large k are based on finite samples, so the magnitude and reliability of the speedups are uncertain.

The gradient-norm analysis (Figure 6) appears to reflect population-level weighting with a large (or infinite) truncation level rather than the finite-$T$ estimator actually used in training (e.g., $T=16$ for Qwen3). For very low pass rates and small $T$, MaxRL's weight is capped near $T$ and can actually be lower than GRPO's $1/\sqrt{p(1-p)}$ weight, so the claim that MaxRL upweights extremely hard prompts more than GRPO requires careful qualification.

The finite-compute MaxRL objective truncates the Maclaurin expansion at $T=N$, which for very hard prompts with $p \ll 1/N$ gives a weight of roughly $N$ rather than the ML weight $1/p$. Thus the method does not fully approximate ML in the extremely-low-pass-rate regime, and prompts with zero successes receive no gradient. The paper acknowledges this but does not thoroughly explore its practical consequences for the hardest tasks.

Several experimental details are inconsistent or confusing: the maze text says training rollouts from 4 to 128, but the figures show 16/128/1024; some figure legends and textual descriptions do not match. These issues make the experimental section harder to parse and reproduce accurately.

strengths: The Maclaurin expansion connecting the maximum-likelihood gradient to a harmonic mixture of pass@k gradients (Eqs. 4-5) is a clean, elegant reframing that makes precise the sense in which expected-reward RL is a first-order approximation of likelihood.

Theorem 2 (estimator-objective equivalence) gives a principled justification for a very simple estimator: averaging score functions over successful rollouts and normalizing by K instead of N. The resulting practical method is a genuinely one-line change to standard RL implementations, which is attractive.

The unifying weight-function view (Section 5, Table 2, Figure 1) is a useful conceptual tool that characterizes ML, RL, GRPO, and MaxRL at the population level and correctly notes GRPO's non-monotone 1/sqrt(p(1-p)) weighting.

The empirical program is broad, spanning a controlled ImageNet setting with exact ML, an infinite-data maze task, a data-scarce GSM8K regime, and Qwen3-1.7B/4B math training, with consistent qualitative trends favoring MaxRL.

The limitations are discussed honestly (binary rewards, zero gradient for prompts with no successful rollout, T=N-1 rather than T=N for the practical estimator), and code/hyperparameters are released.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental relative to concurrent and prior work. Theorem 1 is explicitly acknowledged to overlap with Davis and Recht (2025); the estimator is closely related to rejection-sampling fine-tuning and RAFT (Xiong et al., 2025a) and to pass@k optimization (Walder and Karkhanis, 2025; Tang et al., 2025); and the practical advantage normalization by mean reward is acknowledged to be close to MAPO (Huang et al., 2025). The distinctive contribution is essentially the compute-indexed interpolation framing, which is narrower than the paper implies.

The central framing ('RL is only a workaround to non-differentiability', 'ML is the principled objective') presents a modeling choice as a fact. Expected reward is a legitimate objective with different properties, and the argument that likelihood is uniquely correct in binary-reward settings is asserted rather than established.

The theory is largely tautological by construction: J^(N) is defined as the truncation, and Theorem 2 shows the estimator is unbiased for that truncation. The 'elegant alignment' is a computation rather than a deep result, and the claim that more compute 'improves the objective itself' is conceptually circular because the objective itself changes with N.

The headline empirical claims ('Pareto-dominates existing methods in all tested models and tasks', 'up to 20x test-time scaling efficiency') are not supported with statistical rigor. No error bars or multiple seeds are reported despite the high variance of RL training, and the 20x figure is derived from gaps in pass@k curves under a perfect verifier and is benchmark-specific. The abstract's 'Pareto-dominates' claim is also qualified in the body (MaxRL trails early on GSM8K and only 'matches or outperforms' GRPO on Qwen3).

The practical estimator drops all-zero-pass prompts entirely, so the hardest problems (p < 1/N) receive no learning signal, which is the opposite of the likelihood's intent to upweight hard inputs. The paper notes this but does not resolve it, and the estimator is only unbiased for the (N-1)-truncated objective, further weakening the interpolation story at finite compute.

The comparison against PKPO is suspicious: MaxRL is reported to beat PKPO at pass@16 even though PKPO is explicitly designed to optimize pass@16 (Tables 8-9, Figure 20). The paper offers only a vague hypothesis and no explanation, raising questions about baseline tuning or fairness.

The empirical evaluation focuses mainly on GRPO/RLOO in the main text and reports single training runs for large-scale models, so the claimed reliability of the advantage over alternatives is not well established.

strengths: The theoretical framing is clean and correct: casting binary-reward correctness-based RL as a latent-generation maximum-likelihood problem and deriving the Maclaurin expansion log p = -Σ_k (1-p)^k/k, with standard RL retaining only the k=1 term, is an insightful and well-motivated reframing. The 'first-order approximation' claim is mathematically sound.

Theorems 1, 2, and 5 are correct and carefully proven. The estimator-objective equivalence (that averaging score functions over successful rollouts, normalized by K, is unbiased for the truncated MaxRL gradient of order T=N) is elegant, and the derivation that the practical dropped-baseline estimator is unbiased for order N-1 is a nice, honest piece of analysis.

The method is genuinely simple to adopt: a one-line change to standard RL implementations (normalizing the advantage by per-task mean reward rather than reward standard deviation). This low implementation barrier makes the contribution practically useful.

The empirical evaluation is broad and spans very different scales and regimes: ImageNet classification with an exact maximum-likelihood baseline (validating that MaxRL tracks cross-entropy as compute grows), a 3M-parameter maze transformer with 1M unique tasks (infinite-data regime), SmolLM2-360M on GSM8K (data-scarce regime), and Qwen3-1.7B/4B on math reasoning.

The results are consistent across tasks and models, showing Pareto-dominance over RLOO and GRPO on both pass@1 and pass@k, with pass@k gains that translate into substantial (up to ~20x) test-time scaling efficiency under a perfect verifier.
Reproducibility is handled well: detailed hyperparameter tables, prompt templates, task construction, and an explicit commitment to open-source code and scripts.
The unifying weight-function view (Section 5) is a useful synthesis that places RL, GRPO, MaxRL, and ML on a common footing and clarifies how each reweights hard vs. easy prompts.

The limitations and ethics discussion is honest and specific: the binary-reward restriction, the zero-gradient issue for prompts with no successful rollout, and a preliminary extension to non-binary rewards are all clearly acknowledged rather than glossed over.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic novelty is thin: the method reduces to dividing the advantage by the mean reward instead of the standard deviation, which differs from prior work such as MAPO (batch-mean normalization) mainly in per-prompt vs. per-batch scope. The theoretical results, while correct, are relatively straightforward, and the conditional-gradient identity (Theorem 1) overlaps with concurrent work (Davis & Recht, 2025).

There is a mismatch between the 'principled' objective and what is actually implemented: the practical estimator is only unbiased for order T=N-1, and dropping the gradient entirely for prompts with no successes deviates from the target objective. This gap is acknowledged but not deeply investigated, and it is unclear how it affects the claims of approaching ML.

Normalizing the advantage by the mean reward substantially rescales gradients (for small p, it upweights by roughly 1/p vs. 1/√p for GRPO). It is not disentangled how much of the reported gains come from the objective itself versus an implicit learning-rate/gradient-scale effect; a dedicated ablation controlling for effective step size would strengthen the causal claim.

Some reported gains are extraordinarily large (e.g., maze pass@1 of 84.4 for MaxRL vs. 39.6 for GRPO, and GSM8K pass@1024 of 83.4 vs. 48.8), which raises the possibility of baseline under-tuning or scaling artifacts rather than purely an objective-level advantage. More controlled, compute-matched comparisons (and learning-rate sweeps for baselines) would make the Pareto-dominance claim more convincing.

Improved pass@k during training may partly reflect MaxRL's higher retained entropy and longer chains-of-thought rather than genuine capability expansion. The capability-expansion evidence (Table 10 and the perplexity analysis) is suggestive but rests on a single benchmark with only 30 problems and would benefit from broader support.

The headline test-time scaling efficiency claims (up to 20x) depend on a perfect verifier and on repeated sampling; while the paper notes this, the practical reach of the claim is narrower than the abstract implies.

Minor presentation issues: the contributions list in the introduction is misnumbered (an item begins with '1. [leftmargin=*]' and the numbering starts at 2), and several figures/tables are referenced to appendix material that carries much of the evidential weight.
